Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, with me is Priya from our SE team, priya do you wanna quick wave?
[00:07] Priya: hi! yup, hey folks, excited to walk through the hosted API stuff, we'll keep it practical and show some live curl / sdk snippets and demo streaming.
[00:15] Alex: hi, alex here, thanks. quick context — we're looking at using LLMs for internal clinical documentation and a patient triage assistant, so low latency for some flows and strict data retention rules.
[00:27] Samir: yep, product wants something that can go into our triage workflow, preferrably hosted but may need private eventually.
[00:34] Maya: i'm the ML eng, i'll own the integration, our QPS is modest today ~20 rps but could spike to 150 during launches. Concerned about latency and cost.
[00:45] Jordan: got it, perfect. we'll demo the hosted API — chat and text generation — and focus on streaming, params and the retry behaviour. if it makes sense we can talk dedicated/private afterwards.

[01:05] Priya: quick architecture slide (referenced: link to deck) — hosted API is our fastest path: simple REST + SDKs, model catalog, streaming support and built-in rate limiting. For production we suggest pinning a model snapshot to avoid drift.
[01:30] Alex: do you do model pinning? and what about KV cache or session state? some of our flows need long context (up to 8k tokens).
[01:39] Priya: yes you can pin model versions, and our runtime handles KV cache behind the scenes — it's optimized for variable sequence lengths, you can also enable prefix caching which speeds up repeated system prompts. caveat: caching behaviour slightly depends on model family and quantization.

[02:10] Jordan: demo time — i'll paste a simple curl for chat generation. note: transcription may drop some punctuation in the automated txt but code should copy fine.
[02:22] Jordan: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H "Authorization: Bearer <KEY>" -d '{"model":"redwood-2b","messages":[{"role":"system","content":"You are a helpful assistant."},{"role":"user","content":"Summarize today's triage rules"}]}'
[02:40] Priya: that returns a full response by default but we highly recommend streaming for UI flows. Streaming reduces time-to-first-token and gives progressive rendering.

[03:05] Priya: here's a streaming snippet in node (high-level): client.chat.stream({model: 'redwood-2b', messages: [...], stream: true}) then process events. We emit partial tokens, and an end event. You can do incremental rendering or collect full response.
[03:28] Maya: if streaming, do tokens come reliably in order? any reordering?
[03:33] Priya: generally in order, but network hiccups can cause reconnects — we provide chunk ids and sequence checks so client can dedupe. also we support resume tokens for session style continuation in case of transient disconnects.

[04:05] Jordan: parameters — quick note: temperature controls randomness; lower = deterministic. top_p is nucleus sampling; max_tokens caps length. We also have stop sequences, and presence/ frequency penalties.
[04:22] Samir: what's the recommended defaults for internal doc summarization?
[04:26] Priya: for summarization we usually use temperature 0.0-0.2, max_tokens around 256-512 depending on source doc size, top_p default 0.95 is fine. For creative responses raise temperature.

[05:00] Alex: talk to me about retries — if a request times out or the connection drops during streaming what should our client do so we don't double-charge or get duplicate outputs?
[05:10] Priya: good question. Redwood's hosted API supports idempotency keys on write-ish endpoints. For streaming requests you can attach an idempotency token; if the client reconnects you can either resume from a resume token or request the same idempotency key and we'll dedupe server-side within a short window. For billing, tokens produced are attributed to the successful final response — transient reconnects may produce partial token counts but we surface them in usage logs and billing.
[05:40] Jordan: we also expose per-request metadata and a request_id that helps debug which server handled it — useful for support.

[06:05] Maya: curious about rate limits and throttling — we have spikes, do you offer burst?
[06:12] Priya: yes hosted has soft rate limits and bursts; for steady production at scale we typically recommend Dedicated or reserved capacity. Hosted will gracefully 429 with Retry-After headers; client backoff patterns we recommend are exponential backoff with jitter.

[06:45] Samir: and latency — what latency should we expect for small prompts?
[06:50] Priya: depends on model and seq length; for redwood-2b small prompts ~80-150ms to first token on our best regions, larger models/longer context will be higher. We provide latency SLOs for Dedicated customers.

[07:15] Jordan: i'll demo streaming live — note i'm doing this from a laptop on wifi so forgive any slowness.
[07:25] Jordan: (starts streaming example) [partial chunks omitted] 
[07:45] Jordan: you'll see partial tokens arrive: "In summary, today's triage rules are..." and then more chunks. we demonstrated client-side rendering, ability to cancel mid-stream, and resume.

[09:00] Alex: nice. about security — we need SOC2, data residency in us-east, and bring-your-own-key (KMS/HSM) for certain PHI flows. can you support that on hosted?
[09:14] Priya: hosted supports SOC 2 compliant processes and has region controls; BYOK (KMS) is available on Dedicated and Private. For hosted we can integrate customer-managed keys for encryption at rest in select enterprise plans — there's a short checklist we'll share. also we keep audit logs per request and support SSO / SAML and fine-grained RBAC.
[09:45] Maya: do you store PII or PHI by default?
[09:50] Jordan: default hosted policy is transient retention for 30 days for debugging and improving infra, but we have options to disable retention and purge data; for PHI we typically recommend Dedicated or Private so customers control retention and keys. we'll attach the security doc that details retention windows.

[10:30] Samir: what's the pricing model? token-based? any minimums?
[10:36] Jordan: hosted is usage-based per-token for generation and per-embedding for vector ops. There's a free tier/credits and then pay-as-you-go. Dedicated is committed monthly with predictable throughput. since you mentioned spikes, we can show burst configs or hybrid routing. I'll follow up with a tailored estimate.

[11:05] Priya: back to error handling — examples of HTTP codes: 429 rate limit, 503 transient backend overload, 5xx internals we recommend retry with backoff up to N tries but the client should not blindly retry streams without idempotency keys. Also we support a municipal retry header and you'll see a request_id in response so you can ask support to investigate.

[12:00] Maya: can you show an example with the SDK for stream cancellation and resume?
[12:07] Priya: sure — snippet: const stream = client.chat.stream(...); stream.on('data', chunk => render(chunk)); stream.on('end', () => final()); stream.cancel(); // cancel will emit a cancellation event and server will stop generating. To resume you either reconnect with same idempotency key or send a new request with a resume_token. We'll send resume tokens when generation checkpoints are available.

[13:05] Alex: how large are those resume tokens? any privacy concerns?
[13:12] Priya: they're opaque server-side tokens, not containing customer plaintext. they only reference server state. we can share the short spec in the docs.

[13:40] Jordan: quick demo of parameters — changing temperature live, lower temp gives shorter conservative outputs, higher temp more varied. some of the team laugh cause creative stuff is fun but for clinical you'd keep low.

[15:00] Samir: question about multi-turn sessions: we have session IDs for patients, is there built-in session management?
[15:07] Priya: you can attach session_id metadata and use persistent KV caching on Dedicated to keep context cached; hosted has session tokens too but for very long running sessions or strict privacy Dedicated/Private recommended.

[16:00] Maya: perf benchmarks — do you have public numbers?
[16:05] Jordan: we publish model performance profiles in our docs (link), we also run sample-benchmarks for customers. Priya can help run a quick benchmark with your sample dataset to show cost/latency tradeoffs.

[16:35] Priya: one more note on batching: automatic batching can increase throughput but may add latency to first token; we tune batching based on target SLOs. For interactive triage we keep small batches or streaming to keep TTF (time to first) low.

[17:10] Alex: what about SDKs — do you support python and node?
[17:14] Jordan: yep officially supported client sdks: python, node, and curl examples. we also have community contributed golang libs.

[18:00] Samir: are there quotas or per-key limits? we worry about accidental huge bills from loops during testing.
[18:06] Priya: yes per-key quotas and per-route limits, you can set soft caps and alerts. we also support dev keys with strict limits and production keys with higher quotas.

[18:45] Maya: ok, on security again — do you have SOC2 Type II? audit logs?
[18:50] Jordan: yes SOC2 Type II available; audit logs per request and retention policies are configurable on enterprise plans. we'll attach the SOC2 report and the security whitepaper after the call.

[19:20] Priya: demoing a retry scenario — i purposely drop the connection and reconnect with same idempotency key; server dedupes and we get the final completed response once generation finishes. note: this snippet shows server responding with 202 then streaming.

[20:30] Alex: good. can we limit outputs or enforce safety filters? we must avoid hallucination on clinical output.
[20:36] Priya: we offer model-level safety mitigations and you can run an additional safety classifier or rules post-processing. we also support fine-tuning or prompt engineering to reduce hallucination. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization vs model tradeoffs but for safety you should run evals on prompt-sets and we can hook into regression alerts.

[22:00] Samir: curious about logs and observability — do you provide token-level cost breakdowns?
[22:07] Jordan: yes Console shows token-level cost, per-route latency breakdowns, traces, and you can export logs to cloud storage. we also have webhooks for alerts.

[23:15] Maya: any network requirements for hosted? allowlist IPs, TLS versions etc?
[23:22] Priya: we support IP allowlist for enterprise, TLS 1.2+ recommended, and mutual-TLS available on Dedicated. For hosted we give stable endpoints per region and you can whitelist.

[24:00] Jordan: ok we're coming up on 20 more minutes, want to open for deeper tech questions or cover POC scoping?
[24:08] Alex: i think POC scoping — we want to run a small week-long pilot on hosted with a performance benchmark and a retention config.

[24:25] Priya: suggested POC: 1) share sample dataset and expected QPS, 2) we run a benchmark and generate latency/cost report, 3) security review (SOC2 + retention config), 4) optionally trial a small dedicated pool if spikes need it.

[25:10] Jordan: timeline wise, you said launches could spike around 150 RPS — for that we can do hosted burst but better to plan Dedicated... we'll include cost comparison.

[26:00] Maya: question on shared infrastructure — are there noisy neighbor concerns with hosted?
[26:05] Priya: hosted uses multi-tenant pools but with workload-aware scheduling and pre-emption rules. For strict isolation we recommend Dedicated. Many customers start on hosted and migrate.

[27:10] Samir: ok, what about deployment environments — we need us-east data residency for PHI. By default hosted region selection?
[27:18] Jordan: you can pick region endpoints (us-east, eu-west etc). For PHI/Dedicated we can offer private deployments or on-prem options.

[28:00] Alex: for the POC we need a simple contract/term sheet and an estimate. can you send that?
[28:06] Jordan: yes, i'll send a basic term sheet + pricing and include options for a one month Dedicated trial.

[29:00] Priya: quick note on observability instrumentation — we can add trace ids to responses and integrate with your tracing. also we support per-route dashboards in Console for error rates, token breakdown, and quality regressions.

[30:15] Maya: will you share example prom queries or dashboards?
[30:20] Priya: yes, example dashboards + prometheus queries in the docs bundle we'll send.

[31:00] Samir: any hidden gotchas on streaming and mobile clients?
[31:06] Priya: mobile may need to handle flaky networks; we recommend short keepalive, resume tokens, and small partial renders. also watch for battery/network costs if streaming long responses.

[32:00] Jordan: i'm going to recap next steps — i'll email pricing + term sheet + SOC2 + security whitepaper; Priya will share the streaming code snippets, resume token spec, and benchmark onboarding checklist; Maya will send sample dataset and QPS estimates.

[33:00] Alex: sounds good. expected timelines on attachments?
[33:05] Jordan: i'll get pricing and term sheet by 2026-12-20; Priya will follow up with tech snippets by 2026-12-21.

[34:00] Maya: one more question — what are common mistakes during POC?
[34:05] Priya: common ones: 1) not controlling prompt length so cost balloons, 2) missing idempotency keys so retries duplicate runs, 3) not running safety evals on clinical prompts early, 4) underestimating caching opportunities. We provide a POC checklist to help.

[35:30] Samir: ok. anything about function calling / structured outputs?
[35:35] Priya: yes we support structured outputs via JSON-schema enforcement and function-calling primitives — helpful if you need strict field extraction from clinical notes. We'll demo that in the POC if helpful.
